procedural_history.originating_court: SHO, District Crime Branch, Kancheepuram (registered FIR as Crime No. 21 of 2020)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 15th July 2022 passed by the Single Judge of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in Criminal O.P. No. 20716 of 2020 and Crl. M.P. No. 8763 of 2020.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal O.P. No. 20716 of 2020 before the High Court of Judicature at Madras under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to call for the records and to quash the FIR. The High Court rejected the petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's order, filed a Criminal Appeal No. 1716 of 2024 in the Supreme Court. Notice was issued on 21st October 2022. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed the High Court's order.

directions: The order of the High Court dated 15th July 2022 in Criminal O.P. No.20716 of 2020 and Criminal M.P. No. 8763 of 2020 is quashed and set aside.
The FIR in Crime No.21 of 2020 and the consequential charge-sheet filed against the present appellant shall stand quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: High Court whether justified in rejecting the petition filed by the appellant u/s.482, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

facts: An FIR was registered against the appellant (accused No. 3) and two others for an offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.
The appellant filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) seeking to quash the FIR.
The High Court rejected the petition, stating that the FIR disclosed a prima facie cognizable offence and it could not interfere with the investigation.
Subsequently, a charge-sheet was filed in the case.
The appellant appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court, arguing that even if the allegations were taken at face value, no offence was made out against them.
law: To constitute an offence under Section 420 of the IPC, the FIR/complaint must establish the ingredients of Section 415 IPC, which are: (1) deception of a person, (2) fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property, and (3) a dishonest intention by the accused at the time of the inducement.

The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to prevent the abuse of the process of law is not restricted to the FIR stage. It can be exercised even after a charge-sheet has been filed. The abuse of process is considered aggravated if an FIR materializes into a charge-sheet.
application: The Supreme Court first dismissed the procedural objection that the petition was invalid because a charge-sheet had been filed, affirming that the court's power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. persists.
The Court then examined the FIR and the charge-sheet to see if the essential elements of Section 420 IPC were present specifically against the appellant.
It found that all allegations regarding inducement were directed only against accused Nos. 1 and 2. No role of inducement was attributed to the appellant.
The Court also noted that there was no direct transaction of any nature between the appellant and the complainant.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the 'sine qua non' (essential condition) of dishonest inducement was completely lacking in the case against the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in rejecting the petition. Since the FIR and charge-sheet, even when accepted as true, did not disclose the necessary ingredients for an offence under Section 420 IPC against the appellant, the continuation of criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of law and a miscarriage of justice. Accordingly, the Supreme Court quashed the High Court's order and the criminal proceedings against the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Section 420, IPC, if attracted qua the appellant.

facts: An FIR was registered against the appellant (accused No. 3) and two others for an offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The complainant, at the instance of accused No. 1, transferred Rs. 20,00,000 to the appellant's bank account.
Upon receiving the money, the appellant executed a sale deed in favour of accused No. 1.
The court noted that there was no direct transaction of any nature between the appellant and the complainant.
No further role was attributed to the appellant after the execution of the sale deed.
law: To attract Section 420 of the IPC, the essential ingredients of Section 415 (Cheating) must be established.

The key ingredients are: (1) deception of a person, (2) fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property, and (3) the existence of a dishonest intention at the time of making the inducement.
The court held that "dishonest inducement is the sine qua non" (an essential condition) to attract the provisions of Sections 415 and 420 of the IPC.
application: The Supreme Court examined the FIR and the charge-sheet to see if the ingredients of Section 420 were met with respect to the appellant.
It found that "no role of inducement at all has been attributed to the present appellant."
The allegations regarding inducement were directed only against accused Nos. 1 and 2.
Since the appellant did not induce the complainant to part with any money, the essential element of "dishonest inducement" was "totally lacking" in their case.
The court concluded that even if the allegations in the FIR and charge-sheet were taken at face value, they did not disclose the necessary ingredients to charge the appellant under Section 420 IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Section 420 of the IPC was not attracted to the appellant because the FIR and charge-sheet failed to show that the appellant had played any role in dishonestly inducing the complainant to deliver property, which is an essential ingredient of the offence. Consequently, the court quashed the criminal proceedings against the appellant, deeming their continuation an abuse of the process of law.

arguments.issue_text: High Court whether justified in rejecting the petition filed by the appellant u/s.482, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the High Court was not justified in rejecting the petition under Section 482 CrPC, as the criminal proceedings initiated against them were an abuse of the process of law and the allegations did not constitute an offence.
respondent_arguments: Since the charge-sheet has already been filed, the appeal is rendered infructuous.
The appellant has an alternative remedy of filing an application for discharge.
The High Court was correct in its decision, and no interference is warranted in the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Section 420, IPC, if attracted qua the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the averments in the FIR do not make out a case for the offence of cheating under Section 420, IPC against them.
respondent_arguments: The averments in the FIR clearly show that the appellant, along with other accused persons, has cheated the complainant and defrauded them of a huge amount.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court has inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
obiter: The principles relating to the exercise of jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash complaints and criminal proceedings have been stated and reiterated by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The dishonest inducement is the sine qua non to attract the provisions of Sections 415 and 420 of IPC. In our considered view, the same is totally lacking qua the present appellant. In that view of the matter, we find that continuation of the criminal proceedings against the present appellant would be nothing else but amount to abuse of process of law resulting in miscarriage of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The dishonest inducement is the sine qua non to attract the provisions of Sections 415 and 420 of IPC.

The principles relating to exercise of jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash complaints and criminal proceedings have been stated and reiterated by this Court in several decisions.
policy_considerations: continuation of the criminal proceedings against the present appellant would be nothing else but amount to abuse of process of law resulting in miscarriage of justice.
The power to quash shall not, however, be used to stifle or scuttle a legitimate prosecution. The power should be used sparingly and with abundant caution.
